newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary c.bank to support rates but sees CPI fall.
newsitem.headline: Hungary c.bank to support rates but sees CPI fall.

text.p: The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said it would resist market pressure for a drop in interest rates even though it sees inflation continuing to decline steadily, NBH President Gyorgy Suranyi said on Friday.
Suranyi warned the NBH would intervene if interest rates fell further, in order to keep savings attractive.

"We will not allow interest rates to fall below the realistic level of inflation expectations," Suranyi told a news conference. "Otherwise we would undermine the country's economic stability and would not help a further decline of inflation."
Suranyi said the NBH was determined to support the current interest rate levels, for example one-year Treasury bill yields, which are currently at around 20 percent.

"We are ready to stabilise that interest rate level, and we have all the tools to do so," he said. The bank controls the market rates trough its repurchase operations and through its six-month deposit facility which carries a rate of 20.75 percent.
However, he added that inflation was likely to continue to fall and would allow interest rates to drop later this year.
Suranyi said the consumer price index (CPI) figures for January and February were slightly better than the NBH had expected.
"On the basis of the first two months, there is a good chance that (year-on-year) inflation will have gone down to about 17 percent by December," he added.
Year-on-year inflation was 18.9 percent in January and 18.8 percent in February.
Suranyi said year-on-year inflation may increase slightly in some months of 1997, but saw a steady declining trend for the whole of the year.

He added that the NBH and the Finance Ministry had been commissioned by the government to work on an alternative plan to reduce inflation by more than the originally forecast five percentage points in 1998.

Suranyi said year-on-year inflation could be pushed down to 10 percent by December 1998 if the government and social groups are able to reach a wide-scale agreement on price and wage restraint for next year.

He said that after Hungary cut its budget and current account deficits and real wages substantially in the past two years, high expectations of nominal wage rises remained the major inflationary factor.
"I hope the inflation story in the next few months and years will revolve around the question of wages," he said.
However, he added the government should also raise the issue of the prices of certain goods which influence inflation heavily, including the energy price formula.
Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy has also suggested recently that the energy price formula should be adjusted as elements of the formula generated inflation.

MSZOSZ, Hungary's largest trade union association, said earlier this week that it would be ready to negotiate about reducing inflation in 1998 if the government do not consider nominal wages as the sole factor which triggers inflation.
